speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The amendments proposed today to the Presidential Elections Act can be grouped into three categories.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I will also be making two announcements on the Presidential elections at the end of my speech.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: These announcements do not require amendments to the law.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The amendment Bill was passed in November after robust debate, putting in place the framework for the changes to the Elected Presidency.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The amendments being proposed here today put in place the nuts and bolts of the framework agreed to in November.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I will now take Members through the key changes being proposed.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The new section 5A provides that the new Schedule, inserted by clause 22, has effect for the purpose of determining whether an election is reserved under the new Article 19B(1) of the Constitution.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The new Schedule sets out the terms of office that are counted and the communities that the Presidents who hold these terms belong to.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The first term of office to be counted is the last term of office of President Wee Kim Wee, during which he became the first President to exercise the functions created by the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment) Act 1991.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Schedule stipulates that Dr Wee Kim Wee and Mr Ong Teng Cheong belong to the Chinese community; Mr SR Nathan, who served two terms, belongs to the Indian community, Dr Tony Tan belongs to the Chinese community.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Prime Minister had, in November, announced this during the Second Reading of the Constitutional (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The Returning Officer is responsible for updating the Schedule after every election.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For this purpose, if a community certificate was issued to a person, that person is considered to belong to the community stated on the community certificate.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: If no community certificate was issued to the person, the person is considered not to belong to the Chinese community, the Malay community, nor the Indian or other minority communities.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The new section 5B links the reserved election mechanism in the new Article 19B of the Constitution to writs of election issued under the Act and provides for open elections to be held if a reserved election wholly fails.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: In an open election, a person does not have to belong to any of the three communities − Chinese, Malay, Indian or Other Minority communities − to qualify to be elected as President.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This is an increase from the current five days.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This provides the Presidential Elections Committee (PEC) with more time to assess whether potential candidates should be issued a Certificate of Eligibility.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We are also introducing changes to the certification process for the Presidential election.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The new Division 2 − consisting of new sections 8 to 8D − relates to the PEC and the application process for a Certificate of Eligibility.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, the deadline for applying for a Certificate of Eligibility is extended from the current three days to five days after the date of the Writ of Election.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The extension of deadline will give prospective candidates more time to prepare their applications.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, the PEC must be satisfied that the applicant has met the service requirements under new Article 19(2)(g) of the Constitution before it issues the Certificate of Eligibility.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Third, persons who wish to contest in the Presidential elections must submit applications to both the PEC and to the Community Committee.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: PEC must reject an application for a Certificate of Eligibility if the applicant did not submit a community declaration to the Community Committee.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The community declaration is essential to the functioning of the certification process for the reserved election system.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I will elaborate on the community declaration next.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The community certification process serves two main purposes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: First, to determine the community to which every person elected as President belongs, for the purposes of determining whether a future election is reserved under the new Article 19B(1) of the Constitution.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Second, to ensure that, in a reserved election, only persons belonging to the community to which the election is reserved, qualify to stand for election.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All prospective candidates in all elections, regardless of a reserved election or open election, have to submit a community declaration.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: A declaration is essential even in open elections because the hiatus-triggered model requires that the community of each President to be counted, for the purposes of calculating when the next reserved election is.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: A person making a community declaration must make one, and only one, of the following four statements as set out in the new section 8F(2)(a)-(d).

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, that the person considers himself to be a member of the Chinese community and wishes to apply for a community certificate stating that the person belongs to the Chinese community.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, that the person considers himself to be a member of the Malay community and wishes to apply for a community certificate stating that the person belongs to the Malay community.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Third, that the person considers himself to be a member of the Indian or Other Minority communities and wishes to apply for a community certificate stating that the person belongs to the Indian or Other Minority communities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Fourth, that the person does not consider himself to be a member of the Chinese community, the Malay community, or the Indian or Other Minority communities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The statements require, where the applicant considers himself to be a member of the three main communities, that is, Chinese, Malay, or Indian and Other Minority communities, to state that he wishes to apply for a community certificate stating that he belongs to that particular community.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It should be pointed out that, in open elections, a declarant can still run for elections, even if he does not receive a community certificate, if he meets all other eligibility criteria.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Community Committee must decline to accept a community declaration if the declarant did not apply to the PEC for a Certificate of Eligibility.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The PCMR will make its nominations after consulting such organisations of the Chinese, Malay, or Indian and Other Minority communities as the PCMR sees fit.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The five members belonging to the Chinese community who are on the Community Committee make up the Chinese Community sub-committee.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The same arrangement applies to the Malay and Indian and Other Minority communities' sub-committees.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In a reserved election, the Community Committee will accept a community declaration only if the declarant considers himself to belong to the community to which the election is reserved.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Community Committee will then refer the declaration to the sub-committee for that community.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the sub-committee is satisfied that the declarant belongs to that community, the Community Committee will issue the declarant with a community certificate to that effect.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In non-reserved elections or open elections, the Community Committee will refer community declarations to the appropriate sub-committee, except where a declarant does not consider himself to be a member of any of the three main communities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the sub-committee for a community is satisfied that a declarant belongs to that community, the Community Committee will issue the declarant with a community certificate to that effect.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the sub-committee is not satisfied, the Community Committee can refuse to issue a community certificate, or can invite the declarant to submit another community declaration.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the case of a declarant who does not consider himself to be a member of any of the three main communities, the Community Committee can either accept the community declaration, or invite the person to submit another community declaration.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The approach of the Community Committee and sub-committees, in assessing whether declarants belong to a particular community, should be that of inclusion.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The approach should be to welcome and embrace individuals who identify themselves with a particular community.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This would apply, for example, in cases where declarants are of mixed-race parentage and have significant links with the communities of both parents.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The method of certifying race through community committees has worked well for our Group Representation Constituency (GRC) system; it should similarly serve us well in the Presidential elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 6 amends section 9 to add certain items to the nomination papers that a prospective candidate must submit.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The first item is a statutory declaration in which the prospective candidate declares that he understands the role of the President as set out in the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This ensures that the prospective candidate is aware of the constitutional powers of the President, and is also aware of the constitutional limits of the Presidential office.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It will serve as a declaration to the electorate that the prospective candidate is aware that he should not be drawn into making statements or promises which exceed the constitutionally-prescribed role of the President.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As making a false statutory declaration is an offence, a prospective candidate's submission of the declaration signals that the candidate has studied and understood the responsibilities of the office.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second additional item relates to the community certification process.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In a reserved election, a prospective candidate must submit a community certificate stating that he belongs to the community to which the election is reserved.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In open elections, a prospective candidate who applied for a community certificate in his community declaration must submit either: (a) a community certificate; or (b) the Community Committee's written decision rejecting the application.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: A prospective candidate who did not apply for a community certificate in his community declaration must submit: (a) the Community Committee's written notification that his declaration is accepted; as well as (b) a statutory declaration stating that he does not consider himself to belong to the Chinese community, the Malay community or the Indian or Other Minority communities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This new ground for avoidance is identical to the ground for removing a President in the new Article 22L(3)(e) of the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 20 repeals and re-enacts section 73 to further provide that only PEC can apply to void an election on the ground stated in the new section 71(f).

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is because the false statement, or the omission of the material fact, is made to PEC, and so it would be the appropriate party to apply to the Election Judge to void an election.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These amendments are being made to improve the election procedures.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government is making changes to the design of the ballot paper to improve the process of voting, adjudication and counting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 8 amends section 23 to stipulate that the ballot paper must have a clearly demarcated area for a voter to mark his vote for a candidate.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 10 amends section 25 to state that a voter's mark must only be made in the area demarcated on the ballot paper for that purpose.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This ties in with the amendments to section 33 on how ballot papers are to be adjudicated and counted.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 14 amends section 33 to require the Returning Officer to only consider the marks made by voters in the area demarcated on ballot papers for voters to mark their votes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Under the amended section, if a voter makes a mark outside of this area, the Returning Officer must disregard that mark when determining whether the voter has given his vote to any candidate.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In previous elections, disputes have arisen over whether a mark over a candidate's photo or name should count towards a vote for that individual.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The changes will provide clarity in dealing with these situations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 9 inserts a new section 23A to formalise the inclusion of candidates' photographs on ballot papers and to stipulate the conditions that must be satisfied before a candidate's photograph will be included on that ballot paper.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Photographs of the candidates on the ballot paper were first introduced in the 2011 Presidential election.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This practice has been welcomed by voters, as they were able to more easily identify the candidate they are voting for on the ballot paper.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The amendment Bill also sets out certain actions to deal with contingency situations pertaining to ballot boxes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 12 amends section 32A to empower the Returning Officer to extend the time for the sealed ballot boxes from overseas polling stations to reach Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, the total number of overseas electors is material to the election outcome.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, the Returning Officer is satisfied that any of the overseas ballot boxes are not likely to reach Singapore within the initial 10-day period.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 13 repeals and re-enacts section 32B to remove the requirement for a candidate or his counting agent to apply to the Returning Officer for a recount of votes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: With the amendment, the Returning Officer must carry out a recount of the votes if the criterion for recount is met.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This will avoid unnecessary delays to the recount process.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 15 inserts new sections 36DA and 36DB to deal with the loss or destruction of ballot boxes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The third category of amendments is being made to the Act to align the Act with certain provisions of the Parliamentary Elections Act relating to election advertising, publication of election survey results and exit polls.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clauses 17 and 18 insert new sections dealing with those issues.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 24 makes consequential amendments to the Parliamentary Elections Act in relation to the registration of overseas electors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The consequential amendments are mainly to section 13A of that Act.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This will give overseas voters more time to register or change their allotted polling station.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As I highlighted earlier, I would also like to make two announcements on the Presidential elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The first is on campaign methods and the second on the date of the Presidential elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These two areas will not involve amendments to the law or affect this Bill under consideration.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, the Government will take up the broad thrust of the Constitutional Commission's recommendation on election campaign methods.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In its report, the Constitutional Commission stated, and I quote, "Presidential candidates should be required to conduct their campaigns with rectitude and dignity as befits the office and comports with the unifying role and purpose of the Presidency." The Government fully agrees with the Commission that campaigning for the Presidential election has to be consistent with the President's position as a symbol of national unity.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government also agrees with the Commission that there should be a difference in the campaign methods for Presidential elections and Parliamentary elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As the Commission said, a "Parliamentary election is a contest of ideas and policies, where candidates have to communicate their policies to the electorate and persuade voters as to the strengths of their own proposals as well as the weaknesses of those put forward by other candidates.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This clash of ideas and policies makes for a lively but inevitably divisive contest." The Commission also said, and I quote: (a) "in contrast, candidates for Presidential elections have no policy agenda to advance"; (b) "the President plays no role in setting the national agenda nor does he make policy decisions as to the course that the nation should chart"; (c) " hose are matters which properly fall within the remit of the elected Government"; (d) "there is little, if any, need for the vigorous contest of ideas that takes place during a Parliamentary election".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Commission considered that rules could be enacted which prescribed a "white list" of approved campaign methods, such as televised speeches, and explicitly stated that it was not clear if the holding of rallies is either necessary or helpful in dealing with divisiveness.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government agrees with the Commission that there should be a clear distinction in campaign methods for Presidential elections and Parliamentary elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Campaign methods for the Presidential elections must not inflame emotions and must be in keeping with the decorum and dignity of the office of the President, given the important unifying and custodial roles of the President.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The possibility of changes to campaign rules was raised at the end of the debate on the constitutional amendment Bill last November.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What was clear is that there is support from both sides of this House that campaigning for Singapore's Presidency should be depoliticised and fundamentally different from campaigning during Parliamentary elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government agrees with the Members of this House on our shared goal to differentiate the campaigning methods of the Presidential Elections from that of the General Elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As Presidential elections are contested on a national level and not on a local constituency level, we will encourage the use of platforms and channels that reach out to voters at a national level.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Television enables candidates to have wide national reach, and to broadcast their messages more effectively to the entire nation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the last Presidential Election 2011, there were individual campaign broadcasts and a televised forum.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Candidates can also use the wide array of social media platforms to reach voters.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They can also hold indoor private sessions to engage specific groups of voters.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The format of such indoor private sessions is up to the candidates themselves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is in line with the Government's and Constitutional Commission's position not to encourage rallies, which, by their nature and format, may be divisive and not congruent with the unifying role of the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Nevertheless, candidates who wish to hold rallies may still do so.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They will have to apply to Police for a permit.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Police will assess the application based on public order and security considerations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As there will not be any designated and pre-security assessed rally sites, Police may require slightly more time to evaluate applications to hold rallies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Even though this can be announced closer to the start of the application process, the Government is announcing it early for transparency and prospective candidates' early awareness.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the past, polling day typically fell on the last week of August.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In 2011, the writ was issued in the first week of August.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Campaigning began after National Day and was conducted during the month-long National Day celebrations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Given the slightly longer time required for the new process and to avoid holding Presidential election campaigns during the National Day celebrations period, we will adjust the timing of the polls for the forthcoming elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This resets the clock, so that, in future, Presidential elections campaigning will take place outside of the National Day period, assuming Presidents serve their full six-year terms.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have been advised by the Attorney-General that there can be an interval between the expiry of the incumbent's term and the assumption of office by the new President.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If a new President is not elected by the time President Tony Tan's term expires on 31 August 2017, Article 22N of the Constitution provides for an acting President until a new President is elected and assumes office.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Constitution provides for the Chairman of the Council of Presidential Advisers or, if he is unavailable, the Speaker, to be the acting President.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The acting President, it should be made clear, cannot exercise the functions of the President under Article 22N indefinitely.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have sought the Attorney-General’s Chamber’s (AGC) advice on this proposal to adjust the timing of the polls for the Presidential elections this year.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: AGC has confirmed that this can be done under the current laws.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some Members might ask why the Government cannot simply extend the current President's term to deal with the adjustment to the campaigning period.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: According to Article 20 of the Constitution, the new President shall hold office for a term of six years from the date on which he assumes office.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We cannot extend President Tan's term beyond six years unless we amend the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: (In Malay):   Over the past year, we have received a range of useful feedback from the Malay community and other Singaporeans on the amendments to the elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I am pleased that society, as a whole, understands the objectives and rationale behind the proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We want to maintain and protect our multiracial society because this is what makes Singapore unique.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We want to preserve meritocracy because it is a crucial concept to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Singapore is a country where anyone can fulfil their potential due to their own hard work and abilities, and not because of their ancestry, their connections, their race or their religion.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Therefore, this system that we want to establish will carefully balance two factors − meritocracy and multiracialism.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The same high standards will be imposed on all candidates regardless of race.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This step is taken so that the Presidential election campaign will take place outside the period of National Day celebrations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I hope that eligible Malay candidates will step forward to contest to become a Head of State that can unite our people and provide inspiration to all of us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As a young nation, we must be bold enough to constantly adapt our institutions according to our needs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is the spirit of our Pioneer Generation and that same spirit must always be present in future generations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I will now continue my speech in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: (In Mandarin):   Last November, Parliament passed the Constitution Amendment Bill after three days of intense debate.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Since then, the Government has received feedback from various sectors of society.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Many Singaporeans are very concerned about how we balance meritocracy and multiracialism.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government is heartened to see that the Chinese community, as the majority race, has exercised maturity and showed support for the change.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It demonstrated that our Chinese community uphold the values of multiracialism and inclusiveness.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Singapore is a young nation and our institutions and systems must be adaptable and flexible according to our needs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We should follow the example of our forefathers and do this for the future generations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government agrees with the Constitutional Commission's view that the campaign for Presidential elections must be in line with the unifying role of the President.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All sides of this House support that the campaigning for the Presidential election should not be politicised and should be different from the campaigning during the General Election.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In order to clearly differentiate these two elections, the Government will no longer designate any rally site during Presidential elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Nevertheless, if candidates still wish to hold rallies, they must apply to the Police for a permit.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government will increase the television campaigning time during the elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Candidates can also use social media to reach the voters.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Just as before, they can also hold indoor sessions to engage specific groups of voters.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Campaigning was conducted in August, coinciding with National Day and the National Day celebrations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our laws allow us to do this and our Government institutions are also able to handle this transition period smoothly.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, the amendments I have described today are either consequential to the constitutional amendments made in November, or to improve the processes during elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are drawing closer to our first reserved elections for our President.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The changes to the system have taken more than a year to be discussed and fleshed out since they were first publicly mooted.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In November last year, following the report of the Constitutional Commission headed by Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon, we passed landmark amendments to our Constitution in relation to the elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was to ensure that all the major communities would be represented in the office of elected President.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While there were differences of opinion on whether or not such a "reserved" election was appropriate, almost everyone agreed with the principle that every major community ought to be able to represent the country as President.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, the critics mainly argued that such a system was unnecessary because Singaporeans were unlikely to vote along racial lines and there is no reason to institute such a system.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: During my speech on the constitutional amendments, I had supported the concept of the reserved election because I believed it was a self-correcting safety net.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If the critics were right that race was irrelevant, and members of each of the races were able to prevail in an open election, then this safety net would never be triggered.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, if there was no President of a certain community after five terms, then it would be triggered, and hopefully, a person of that community would come forward.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the long run, as Singaporeans get used to having Presidents of different communities, hopefully, race will matter less and minority candidates would start winning open elections, making the reserved election mechanism redundant.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This Bill before Parliament makes the consequential changes to the Presidential Elections Act to implement, among other things, the concept of the reserved election.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It also creates a Chairman for this Committee.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For each of the committees, the Presidential Council for Minority Rights is required to consult such community organisations as it sees fit.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is slightly unusual drafting because the typical constitutional convention is for the President to act on the advice of the Prime Minister, whereas this particular provision requires the Prime Minister to appoint based on the nomination of the Presidential Council for Minority Rights.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One clarification I wish to seek from the Minister is whether this is a decision in which it is intended that the Prime Minister is to exercise discretion, in which case it is expected that the Presidential Council for Minority Rights would put forward more than one nominee for the post as Chairman, from which the Prime Minister will select one, and more than five individuals for each of the five sub-committees from which the Prime Minister will select five.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, if the intention is to leave this decision to the Presidential Council for Minority Rights, then they may only nominate one person for the position of Chairman, and five for each of the sub-committees, in which case it appears the Prime Minister will have no discretion on this matter.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Next, let me move to a new section 8F which sets out the mechanism by which the race of a candidate is to be determined.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The mechanism starts with the candidate self-declaring the community to which he considers himself to be a member.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The appropriate sub-committee then decides if it agrees with the declaration.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Thereafter, there is also a mechanism permitting the Committee to ask the candidate to re-apply if it is of a different opinion.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Naturally, the mechanism is left flexible to deal with the complexity of race.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Thus, a Chinese person adopted at infancy by an Indian family may grow up identifying themselves as part of the Indian community, despite their ethnicity − indeed, interracial adoptions were common, particularly during the baby boom years when parents were unable to take care of all their children.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: People of mixed descent may face more challenges and as interracial marriages get more common.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, I understand the number has doubled from the last decade.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Would it be possible, for example, for a person of mixed heritage, say Indian-Malay, to believe they belong to more than one community?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, this would be the aspiration from the perspective of racial integration and permitting dual-ethnicities is logical if the person is able to identify with both communities and is accepted by both communities, but this may mean that dual-identities may then need to be recorded.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is a problem that, perhaps, may not be faced in the immediate future because we have several terms before the next reserved election.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But it is one that we should prepare for.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The reserved election for Indians and Other Minority communities, in particular, may create issues in this regard.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is a common belief that this category includes everyone who does not fit into the other categories.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This appears to be the intention of this Bill as well since section 8F(2)(d) allows the person to declare he does not identify with any of the communities above.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think this is fair because the purpose of this reserved election is to ensure that all of our main communities feel represented in the highest office and, if a person is not part of a particular community, then they should contest in the open election.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What this means is that the definition of "Other Minority" communities is potentially a prickly matter.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If the Minister is also able to identify, of course, without limiting which groups may fall into the category of such communities at this point in time, that may also be helpful guidance as to what considerations need to be taken into account in determining whether a person is part of one of the "Other Minority" communities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Race is never a pleasant topic because we all like to believe that we live in a place where race does not matter.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, minorities experience disadvantages all the time and it is heartening to know that active steps are being taken to ensure minority representation is possible at all levels, including the office of President.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is my hope that we will one day reach a stage when a member of any race can contest and win the Presidential election without the need for a reserve election, but until we get there, this is a helpful way to ensure that members of each community get a chance to prove themselves in the highest office and help us move towards that ideal.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: (In Tamil):   Mdm Speaker, I will say a few words in Tamil on this Bill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This Bill marks the consequential legislative amendments to implement the Constitutional changes to the elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the important features is the mechanism to ensure that all the major racial groups in Singapore will have a chance to hold this office.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While being a minority in any country has its challenges, in Singapore, steps are taken to confront the challenges wherever possible to ensure that we have proper representation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Tamil is one of the four official languages, and Singapore is one of the few places where Tamil can be used in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In Parliament, the GRC system has ensured that Malays, Indians and other minority groups have always had a place and a position to speak up.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These new changes now ensure that even at the office of President, Indians and other minorities will have a good chance to be represented.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It may be some 25 years before the reserved election for Indians comes up, and it may be that if an Indian gets elected as President before that, we may not even need the reserved election, but it is good to know that we have a system in place, should it ever be necessary.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party rejects both these concepts and thus opposed the Bill then.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As this Bill today seeks to entrench these further, we oppose this Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Lest we be misunderstood or misconstrued, I should state once again that we wish to see multiracial representation in the office of our Head of State.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, such multi-racial representation should be achieved not by way of reserved elections but by the former system of appointing Presidents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We have canvassed our arguments during the debate on the Constitution amendments and we do not intend to rehash them today.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, how to count reserved elections and, secondly, the eligibility criteria of candidates from the private sector.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 3 introduces a new section 5A that to determine whether an election is reserved under Article 19B of the Constitution, one has to refer to the new Schedule.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To recap, during the November debate, the Prime Minister told the House for the first time that the Government had received advice from AGC on how to apply the hiatus-triggered mechanism for reserved elections, that is, which President's term to count from.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We were told that the advice was that counting should begin from President Wee Kim Wee, who was the first President to exercise the powers of an Elected President.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This advice was surprising and illogical to many Singaporeans, given that President Wee Kim Wee was never elected to office.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When I asked Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean then whether the Government would publish the AGC's advice for Singaporeans to better understand the reasoning, the Government appeared reluctant to do so and even asked me whether I was suggesting that the Prime Minister was not being truthful.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There has been a lot of public reaction to the announcement that this year's Presidential election would be reserved for Malay candidates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After the last Presidential elections six years ago, Singaporeans are right to be sceptical about the Government's motives now.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In 2011, Dr Tony Tan was the Government's preferred choice but had to fight off three other candidates, scrapping through to victory with a mere 35.2% of the popular vote and a razor-thin margin of 0.35%.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For the next Presidential election, we hear a sudden announcement by the Government that it would be reserved for Malay candidates based on reasoning which is totally unconvincing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How many people really believe that the Presidential election this year is reserved for Malays to ensure minority representation and why now?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have been reflecting on the decision to use President Wee as a reference point.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I realise that this decision to count from President Wee was not a matter of getting legal advice to interpret any existing laws.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If one looks at this Bill and the Schedule, the Government is asking Parliament to simply make it the law that President Wee is the first one to be counted.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Why not count from the first Elected President, Mr Ong Teng Cheong?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is it because if President Ong was the first one to be counted, we would have to go through this year's elections as an open election and risk the contest by Chinese or Indian candidates who may not be to the Government's liking?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is the decision to count from President Wee not an arbitrary and deliberate decision of the Government to achieve a desired outcome?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 3 also introduces a new section 5C which deals with the eligibility criteria for Presidential candidates from the private sector.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Basically, nothing but to say that Parliament is delegating its legislative authority to the Minister to make regulations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But what disturbs me is that these definitions are not just technical or operational.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These definitions would determine who gets to run for President.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, if one refers back to the Constitution (Amendment) Bill passed in November, it was provided in the new Article 19(6) that it is the Legislature that is supposed to specify how the PEC is to determine the value of shareholders' equity and profit after tax, and it is the Legislature that is supposed to specify what constitutes an insolvency event.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Since the Constitution entrusts these specific matters to the Legislature to deal with, it is not right for Parliament to simply delegate this responsibility to the Minister to do so.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Parliament should not abdicate its responsibility and give a blank cheque to the Government to draw up these definitions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We will later call for our dissent to be specifically recorded.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Speaker, the President is the symbol of our country and has to unite all Singaporeans regardless of race, language or religion, working together for the country's prosperity and progress.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I have three suggestions with regard to the amendments to the Presidential Elections Bill.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: First, regarding the neutrality and fairness of the selection process.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The 16 individuals are the so-called inspectors during the election process.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, the selection of the committee members should be done with great care.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding their ethnicity, these 16 individuals must be equipped with fundamental qualities, such as values, character, capabilities and, especially, good standing in their particular ethnic community.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Ideally, they should not belong to any political party; some should have served a long time in community organisations or business chambers.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: They should be familiar with social matters and have opportunities to interact with people from various backgrounds and have a wealth of experience in community engagement.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: They should belong to different age groups and should have young people among them.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: New media is now predominant, and the presentation and rules of the game vary greatly between the real world and the virtual world.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: To include in the Committee young people with stable values, who are conversant with Internet technology and have an interest in social issues, will enable their views to wield more influence in every sector of society and in the new media.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: As for the other criteria for members of the Committee, I hope the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) will consolidate the feedback from the community at large before deciding on a complete set of criteria.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Interracial marriages and bringing in new immigrants will bring about ethnic integration.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Winning the respect of the community depends on one's character and behaviour.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: If there is an outstanding individual who has superlative abilities and is willing to serve the society, even if his or her parents are of different ethnic groups, surely both communities will be proud of him or her.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, if a person has reprehensible character and conduct, no group will find him acceptable.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We have to pay attention to the selection process of the Presidential candidates.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Besides ethnicity, character and capability are even more important.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, should there be any candidates originating from interracial background participating in the next presidential election, I hope the Committee could give careful considerations when confirming the community that they belong to, to avoid losing talents.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The third suggestion is to extend the nomination and campaign period.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Being a Chinese, I am not familiar with developments within the Malay community and there are many Chinese voters like myself.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: During the last Presidential election, I took a taxi to the airport.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: On the way, the taxi driver said something which has left a deep impression on me.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: He said, "The President has to represent Singapore to meet leaders of different countries and his photograph will be hanging on the wall for five years.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: His wife's photograph will also be displayed for five years.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We must elect someone who is pleasing to the eye." While this may sound simplistic, it does reflect the views of the general public towards the Presidential election.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Presidential elections and Parliamentary elections are very different.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Many of the candidates who run for General Elections have served in the grassroots for a long time and have had direct interactions with the voters.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Some newer candidates have also been mentored by senior Members of Parliament (MPs) and have an all-rounded understanding of the roles, responsibilities and the working process.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The number of MPs is large and they are from diverse backgrounds as well, enabling them to get the support from voters of different backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, for the coming election, the candidates can only be a Malay.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: If the election period is short, many may not be interested in the election because they are not familiar with the background of the candidates.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that gold will always shine and talent will always obtain trust.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, as the issue pertains to the population at large, they do need time to understand the candidates.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: We feel that meritocracy and multiracialism are the two pillars of Singapore's success.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's style of government has been tried and tested over the years.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The business community is most concerned about social stability and racial harmony; only then can economic growth be ensured.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I support the amendment to the Presidential Elections Bill and hope that it can be refined continuously.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party believes that Singapore is best served by an appointed President and a system that will allow the Government to appoint a President regardless of race or religion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With the prospect of reserved elections for minorities, it should be reasonable to assume that the Government expects form to follow function.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It cannot be the Government's intention that a bare declaration that a candidate considers himself or herself to be part of a particular community as stated in clause 8(f) would carry overwhelming weight for candidature to the highest office in the land.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, clause 8(g)(4) states that the Committee must be guided by the merits of the application by a prospective Presidential candidate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But what defines a meritorious application and on what basis will an application be deemed so?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What factors are assessed to determine if an applicant sees himself or herself as a member of particular community?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To begin with, and in step with the Government's decision to institute reserved elections, the Government must concede that language is an important criterion that is intricately tied to race.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, does a minority applicant's language abilities in his or her Mother Tongue matter to the relevant community sub-committees the same way it does for Singaporean students through their educational journey?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would an applicant be expected to have passed his or her Mother Tongue at the GCE "O" and "A" levels?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, should a Presidential candidate who sees himself as part of the Indian community pass muster if he or she can barely get by in Tamil or the other Ministry of Education-recognised Indian languages?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister confirm if language proficiency is a consideration for the Community Committee and, if it is not, why not?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Former Speaker of Parliament, Mr Abdullah Tarmugi, put it differently when he told The Straits Times about his possible candidacy in the upcoming reserved Presidential elections, and I quote, "I will be lying if I say that friends have not been asking me about it… If you look at the people who qualify, it is not that big a pool… I have got to think of my own preferences, my life, my family and my privacy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is not a journey I take myself." The last point is worth repeating and it needs to be stressed: This is not a journey I take myself".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On that note, has the Government deliberated whether the background of an aspiring President's spouse is a factor for the Community Committee's consideration in assessing whether that applicant is a member of a particular community?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, in the case of an interracial marriage, what if the spouse of the applicant does not see himself or herself to be part of the Indian community whereas the aspiring Presidential candidate does?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What if a spouse has converted to Islam in order to marry but does not partake in the practices of the faith?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Should there be residual doubts about how the Community Committee makes its decisions, the presidency could be anything but a unifying office not just for Singaporeans in general but the respective minority race in particular.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A third aspect of the Community Committee I wish to clarify with the Minister is whether the Community Committee would expect an applicant to be active in community work and what this entails.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This expectation has also been referred to by one academic who was quoted in the media as saying that if an applicant has not been, and I quote, "in the public eye, and is not active in community work, it is much harder to make the case for seeking election to the highest office of the land." What are the expectations of community service amongst the candidates and, if so, are the expectations the same with regard to all four classes of candidates, namely, public sector, public sector deliberative track, private sector and the private sector deliberative track?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fourthly, during the recent debate on the Constitution, one People's Action Party (PAP) MP suggested that the presidency ought to be reserved for individuals born in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government did not address this point during the debate but perhaps it can today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Government at least affirm that the PEC shall not issue a certificate of eligibility to any male candidate who has not performed two years of National Service?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would be in line with the reality that National Service brings Singaporeans of all races together towards a common purpose and would serve as an important foundation for the life experience of any future President.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This may render hollow the Government's claims that it is not relaxing the criteria to make it easier for minorities to assume the presidency as a result of the latest constitutional changes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If so, the more accurate statement would be that the stringent private sector requirements simply do not apply for public sector track or public sector deliberative track candidates, minority or otherwise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Government set out its position on this matter in light of the introduction of reserved Presidential elections?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: This Bill proposes to put in place nuts and bolts to give effect to these changes and to improve election procedures.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In this connection, I would like the Minister to confirm if the smallest unit to which electors are allotted in our Presidential Election is the ballot box, a unit smaller than the polling station.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: If so, I would like to make the following points on election procedures.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: On the abandonment of counting, the Bill provides that in the event a ballot box is lost or destroyed in transit, the counting of all the votes cast at the affected polling station, including the votes cast that were not in the lost or destroyed ballot box, would be abandoned.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: If electors are allotted to the level of ballot boxes, should we not provide that any re-vote would take place only if the total number of electors affected by the lost or destroyed ballot box, rather than the entire polling station, proved material?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In other words, why not limit as much as we can the electoral impact of any lost or destroyed ballot boxes?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: It is not unreasonable to expect that fewer than 4,000 electors allotted to an affected polling station and another 4,000 electors registered to vote overseas, would trigger a re-vote at the polling station in a close election under the proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Why give leverage to persons who tamper with the ballot boxes seeking to influence the results of our Presidential Elections?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Why amplify their powers to do so in close elections?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: How about the manner in which the polling would be restarted once it has been determined that the affected number of votes is material?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Currently, in a different context, our laws provide that polling may be abandoned and restarted on another day in our Presidential or Parliamentary Elections in the case of riot or open violence, storm, flood, fire, fire, health hazard or some other difficulties in the physical conduct of voting.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In such cases, our laws provide that the abandonment and the restart of polling must be carried out in the prescribed manner and among other things, only those electors who "have not already voted", shall be entitled to vote when the polling restarts.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In contrast, in the Bill before us today, it is not clear to me if electors who have voted at the polling station and whose ballots remain available for counting because they are not in the lost or destroyed ballot box, whether they would also vote again when polling restarts in this case.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Instead, the Bill says, "The Minister may prescribe the manner in which the abandonment of the counting of votes, the restart of polling, or the counting of votes is to be carried out".

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: And if the Minister indeed has that discretion, is that not too much discretion, especially in a close election?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   Following the Prime Minister's announcement early last year about the proposal to review the Elected Presidency, a Constitutional Commission was formed to study this matter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This Commission submitted a very detailed Report and suggested several changes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Report was then studied by the Government, which also produced a White Paper as its response to the Report.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The issue of the review to the Elected Presidency was intensively debated within and outside of Parliament.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have now reached the stage where we amend the Presidential Elections Act.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Nonetheless, I feel that it is important for us to think about the fundamental issues that were raised during the debates on the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Regardless of any view on this matter, we cannot deny that the discussions that we had together as one people have sparked an awareness about the important things in our lives within a multiracial society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have not reached the ideal state where everything is perfect, and the efforts to forge interracial relations is a work-in-progress, especially in the context of an ever-changing world.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We can see the challenges in other countries, and we need to prepare our people to overcome those challenges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Here, I would like to take the opportunity to echo what was stated by Minister K Shanmugam recently.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: During a discussion at the symposium organised by the S.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS), he asked that Singaporeans, as a society, remain committed in protecting our minorities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He also spoke about how minorities should also play their part and not become exclusive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This view is stated in the context of discussing the issue of xenophobia and extremist views.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, I feel that this message shows how important it is for us to always be sensitive and conscious of the collective responsibility to continue efforts to strengthen interracial relations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, although we may have different views on other issues, we can come together and resolve to preserve our identity as a multiracial society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): Following the Prime Minister's announcement on the proposal to review the Elected Presidency, an independent Constitutional Commission conducted a thorough review which culminated in a very detailed report.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This report not only gave me an insight into the diversity of views on the matter, but also a better understanding of the Elected Presidency in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In the wake of the Government's White Paper in response to the Constitutional Commission Report, I engaged in numerous discussions with many Singaporeans on the issue in my personal capacity, and as well as an MP.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I had shared my reflections and observations during the debates at the Second Reading of the Constitution (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: After a very intensive debate during that Reading, the Bill was passed, and we are already now looking at the specific amendments in the Presidential Elections (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I just have several clarifications and observations which I wish to make.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Commission had, among other things, proposed that there be rules to regulate campaigning methods, with a view to tempering divisiveness of the election process and ensuring that campaigning remains consistent with the role of the President as a symbol of national unity and which preserves the dignity associated with the highest office of the land.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Commission had also proposed that certain laws be enacted for candidates to make explicit declaration on their understanding of the constitutional role of the President, make it an offence for candidates to make promises or take positions that are incompatible with the office of President and impose a regime of sanctions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am also happy to hear that there will be some adjustments made to allow for more national airtime for the Presidential candidates.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These are useful measures in the right direction to regulate campaign conduct.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We are not race-blind, we are not there yet.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The discussion on minority representation for the Elected Presidency system has created an openness to talk about something that used to be perceived as a sensitive topic, such as race.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It made us a bit uncomfortable to think about the current state of affairs but it had pushed us to think about issues a bit more.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What is heartening for me is that at the core of the discussions is a great desire to see Singapore embrace its multiracial, multicultural and multi-religious identity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There was a firm acknowledgment of our commitment to make Singapore a place for all races, and I think this is worth reflecting on and would be a galvanising force to rally people to decide on what is best for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should continue to take positive steps to work towards our vision of being race-blind.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe that with the continued effort, we can and will make Singapore a place where the people remain united, regardless of race or religion.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.45 pm.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.28 pm until 4.45 pm.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: When I was in London late last year, I had the opportunity to have dinner with some MPs of the United Kingdom (UK) from both the Labour and Conservative parties.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We discussed several issues, including why the majority of UK's European Union (EU) Referendum's opinion polls were wrong.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many reasons were cited, including the following: (a) opinion polls predicted that the majority of UK residents would vote against Brexit to stay in the EU.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But these results were skewed as a significant group of the Brexit camp did not voice their true opinions in the surveys.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: They did not want to be perceived as being anti-EU when the mainstream media and experts were saying otherwise; (b) this lulled the "Remain" camp into a state of complacency and many chose not to vote, thinking it would be a safe result.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In short, opinion polls are very prone to errors.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: More importantly, the opinion poll results clearly affect the behaviour of the voters before polling day.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Election surveys are exciting, newsworthy and lucrative to the companies that conduct the survey but may not be helpful.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The British and Americans are so used to election surveys that it would be hard to ban them.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For Singapore, it is best not to start having election surveys.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is a uniquely Singapore phenomenon, and so is the reserved election.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: When would the prescribed form be released to the public?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Why is there a need for an additional requirement?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: What would be the consequences if a Presidential candidate, during his or her campaign, says things or makes election promises that contravene certain aspects of the President's role under the Constitution?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Would the candidate be disqualified during the campaign or after the campaign when the candidate has already won the election?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Or would the candidate be able to get away with a fine only after polling day?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For that matter, I had wanted to ask what would be the changes to the election rules that govern the Presidential Election prior to the Minister's speech during the Second Reading.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I am glad that the Minister has made two announcements regarding the Presidential Election, especially the election rules.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is a worthy move that makes it more transparent, upfront and give all stakeholders ample time to clarify, adapt and comply.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Speaker, the President holds the highest office in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Hence, the Presidential elections should be different from local elections.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The Presidential candidates need to reach as many Singaporeans as possible within a short period of time, and the best channel is through TV broadcast.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Just as I was pondering asking the Minister when the new election regulations would be announced, Minister Chan revealed them at the Second Reading.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, I am glad that he has made the announcement early to make it more transparent and fair.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It also allows potential candidates to have ample time to prepare.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I noted that the Minister did not specify the frequency of the TV broadcast.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: At the same time, there should be at least two live telecast debates among the candidates so as to give Singaporeans enough opportunities to assess the candidates' capabilities and persuasiveness.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I hope the Minister can consider this suggestion.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In today's digital age, the candidates can always go online and use various social media platforms to reach the voters.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Although TV broadcast and online communications allow the candidates to engage the voters extensively, many Singaporeans would still prefer to see the candidates in person.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Certainly, the candidates could go to shopping malls or hawker centres during peak hours to meet and talk to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If that is permissible, I hope that the Police can simplify the application procedures.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I understand that it is not possible for the candidates to meet every voter face to face.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Nonetheless, I hope that under the new election rules, Presidential candidates could still have the option to access large sites for the purpose of having live interaction with the masses.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We know that the coming Presidential election will be reserved for the Malay community for the first time.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If we follow the previous election schedule, polling day may conflict with the Hajj period.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I also have some questions regarding the functions and responsibilities of the Acting President.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Does the Acting President have the same powers as the Elected President?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If so, some critics might have conspiracy theories that the Government will, in this interim period, ask the Acting President to approve the use of the Reserves or make key appointments such as the Police Commissioner or Chief Justice.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is to preempt such rumours from surfacing in the first place.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: At the same time, I hope that the Minister could ensure that Presidential candidates are not denied the opportunity to meet the masses face to face during the campaign period.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, I would like to seek a few clarifications and also offer some suggestions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that the decision-making process of the Community Committee can be transparent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I trust that the Community Committee will carry out its functions in a fair and equitable manner.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, there should be no issues and difficulties in allowing the decisions and processes to be transparent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In today's liberal social media where opinions and questions are openly raised and disseminated, it would be advisable for the Government to provide answers and clarity, before doubt and misinformation cloud the minds of people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To this end, the Community Committee should be transparent in its processes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have as well additional reasons for suggesting why the Community Committee should reveal the reasons that guided it to the conclusion to reject a declaration form.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, the declarant does not appear to have any recourse if he or she believes the decision made by the Community Committee is incorrect or unjustly concluded.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, it would be considerate to produce the reasons behind the rejection in order to demonstrate that the Community Committee considered the form and relevant documents or evidence rigorously and fairly in an application where the declarant has probably only one chance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Thirdly, the Community Committee, which is statutorily unencumbered by legal forms or evidence laws as per section 8G(4), appears to be able to make its decision with fewer considerations or constraints.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, it would be helpful for the declarant and the public to know of the reasons behind the rejection.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would surely help preserve the credibility of the Community Committee.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I note that the Community Committee may regulate its own procedure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Could the use of this power be clarified and what possible regulations of procedure do we envisage?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The phrase "any proceedings" appear to include decisions on accepting or rejecting a declaration form.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As a group of persons who are not democratically elected by the citizens of Singapore, it is only appropriate for the PEC to account to the electorate on the reasons that guided the PEC to limiting the nominees to such persons only.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The principles underlying the changes were passed by the House last year, and the debate on those changes have passed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is not the place to reignite those debates.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I hope that the debate would take place on the changes in the Bill today.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: With that, let me deal with the specific matters raised by the Members.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These can be grouped into two broad sets of issues.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The first set of issues relates to the Community Committee provisions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second set of issues relates to the election processes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If I have time, I will cover some of the queries on the campaigning method and the timing of the election.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, let me thank Ms Rahayu Mahzam for making the points that it is important for us to make efforts to maintain our multiracial and multicultural identity, and that we need to always take care of the rights of minorities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will continue to work hard to ensure that each Singaporean feels cherished in our society, regardless of which community they are from.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Rahayu also had a question on whether an applicant can request for a further invitation to submit a community declaration upon rejection.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As the proposed new section 8H(9) points out, the invitation comes from the Community Committee and is unsolicited.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I also thank Mr Thomas Chua for raising two points in his speech relating to the Community Committee.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The five members who belong to the Chinese community are to be appointed by the Prime Minister on the nomination of the Presidential Council for Minority Rights (PCMR) after consulting such organisations of the Chinese community as the Council sees fit.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This will ensure that the views of the Chinese community will be taken into account in the nomination process.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, the Government also agrees with Mr Thomas Chua that qualified persons must not face difficulties with applications for community certificates simply because they are of mixed parentage.
