speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If a citizen whose parents belong to two different communities decides to run and decides to apply for a community certificate, the relevant community sub-committee should adopt an inclusive attitude towards his application.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I would also like to thank Mr Louis Ng for the two suggestions he made in his speech.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, I agree with Mr Ng that the process should be as transparent as possible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are amending this Bill first before setting out the necessary regulations governing how the PEC and the Community Committee will conduct their meetings.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Constitutional Commission suggested that we adapt the mechanism for determining a prospective candidate's community from the Parliamentary Elections Act, and the mechanism in the Parliamentary Elections Act does not require the Community Committee to release grounds.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This has worked well over the years and we see no need to disturb this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, Mr Louis Ng suggested that the PEC should set out its reasons for rejecting a candidate.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Indeed, the Constitutional Commission said that "it would be desirable for the PEC to give reasons when it rejects applications for Certificates of Eligibility", as this will "provide a measure of transparency and accountability to the process." However, the Commission did not think that the PEC should publicise its reasons for rejecting an application, because that could discourage persons from stepping forward to run for office, for fear of the embarrassment of being rejected in their application for a Certificate of Eligibility and then having the reasons for the rejection made public.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As this is governed by subsidiary legislation, we will proceed to amend the relevant regulations after this Bill is passed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Vikram Nair made two points in his speech.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, he asked about the Prime Minister's appointment of the members of the Community Committee upon the nomination of the PCMR.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The intention under the new section 8E is for the PCMR to nominate one person for the position of Chairman and five for each of the sub-committees, and the Prime Minister will appoint them to the Community Committee accordingly.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This mirrors the approach taken with regard to the nomination of the Chairman and Members of the Malay Community Committee and the Indian and Other Minority Communities Committee by the PCMR and their appointment by the President, as set out in the Parliamentary Elections Act.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, Mr Vikram Nair sought a clarification that the "other minority communities" provision is not intended to be a catch-all for people who do not fit into other categories by ethnicity, but is intended to be only for those who are part of the established minority communities in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: He also asked about which groups may fall into the category of such communities at this point in time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, she asked, as she did last November during the debate on the changes to the Constitution, about the advice from AGC to the Government on the counting of terms.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the same debate, Deputy Prime Minister Teo had confirmed to Ms Lim that the advice referred to by the Prime Minister in his speech was, indeed, AGC's advice, and invited Ms Lim to challenge it judicially if she thought that it was not correct advice.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Lim then suggested that there might be something controversial or confidential that the Government was unwilling to publish.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government is confident of the advice rendered by the Attorney-General.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We proceeded on that basis during the debates on the constitutional changes in this House.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Prime Minister Lee explained to all why we needed the hiatus-triggered mechanism, and we passed the Constitution (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are here today to put the nuts and bolts in place for a decision made clear by the Prime Minister during the debates in November.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we will not go through this again.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I have also gone round to solicit feedback from the public.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I am rather bewildered that Ms Lim is bewildered, because I did not receive the sentiments that Ms Lim said she got.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The feedback that I have received has not been like that.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And if I may just make two points.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Lim once again questioned the Attorney-General's advice.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Or (b) that the Prime Minister has not been truthful with the Attorney-General's advice?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If it is the first, then I think Ms Lim, as suggested by Deputy Prime Minister Teo, can challenge this in the Courts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But if it is the second, then I am afraid it is a very serious issue to cast aspersions on the integrity of our Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Lim is a lawyer; I am not a lawyer.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: You will know that when you get advice, you do not freely publicise your advice and you may have various reasons why you do not publicise all your advice.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And as a lawyer, I think Ms Sylvia Lim will know this better than me.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I think we should not impute motives on this Government or the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On Ms Lim's second point, the proposed amendments state that the Minister must have regard to, to the extent that they are applicable, the prevailing accounting standards and the general law relating to the insolvency of companies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And if you think about it, is this not even better than the Minister setting the rules by himself?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are adhering to the prevailing accounting standards set by the professional bodies and not by someone else outside the profession.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, if you ask me, I think this is an even stronger system than that proposed for the Minister to decide.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, on language proficiency and other criteria, Mr Singh spoke about how it is up to the Community Committee to look at the prospective candidate holistically, and not home in on one factor.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is not new; it has worked well in the GRC context.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, as to whether the President has to be born in Singapore, we should be careful in differentiating between new citizens and those who are born in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They are entitled to exercise their rights and are expected to live up to their responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The question of whether a new citizen is accepted as a unifying symbol of Singapore is one that should be left to the electorate to decide.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If I may refer Members to the Hansard, in 2001, then-Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong, in answering a question by Mr JB Jeyaretnam, had stated that "The First Lady is not a position enshrined in the Singapore Constitution.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is a courtesy term that has been customarily used for the wife of the President, including previous Presidents, before the Elected Presidency was created." Fourth, Mr Pritam Singh asked about the GRC system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is totally unrelated to the Bill today but, since it was raised, I will deal with it.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When Mr Goh Chok Tong moved the Motion to explain the GRC system to this House, it was done with a very clear intent to achieve two purposes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One, it was to ensure that this House has sufficient minority Members in the House as a system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is more than what you would expect proportionally from adding up the percentage of Malays, Indians and Other Minorities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, that was the first purpose ‒ to make sure that this House has sufficient minority represented.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And, over the years, we have achieved this by leaning forward and having more than the minimum that we are expected to have.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second reason for the GRC system was to make sure that none of the parties will campaign on issues on a race/religion platform, that we will all, regardless of party lines, campaign on the basis that we are all Singaporeans, that we will not use race, language or religion for political reasons.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These were the two very clear reasons why we established the GRC system in this House.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Members of the GRC team who are elected to serve their respective GRCs are expected to serve all their residents, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Goh Chok Tong was further asked: if one Member of the GRC team resigns or for whatever medical reason is incapacitated, does the GRC need to hold a by-election?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And the answer was given that it is no, because, recalling the two specific reasons that we set up the GRC system: one was to ensure that this House has sufficient minority representation and, given our current circumstances, we have more than what we would expect by a pure proportional representation system; two, the aim was to make sure that no parties campaigned on the issues of race, language or religion; and three, all Members of the GRC team are expected to serve all their residents regardless of race, language and religion.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But since it was asked, I will put on record our reply.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Fifth, let me talk about public sector candidates which Mr Pritam Singh raised.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I do not think the public sector candidates lack experience.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Whether it is a public sector candidate or a private sector candidate, they all bring with them their respective suite of experience to the office of the President.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They are senior people who have been exposed to a broad range of social, economic and security issues and they would likely have managed and led substantial organisations and regularly made decisions impacting thousands, as the Commission had noted.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These officers would have "experienced the contrary pulls and pressures of Government decision-making".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Before I leave this point about the process, I also want to touch on one point which Ms Sylvia Lim raised.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Lim, in her speech, seemed to have suggested or imputed that this Government has all sorts of short-term political objectives to amend the Constitution and put in place this new system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Can I put it to the Member that this is not the style of this Government?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are here to build for the long haul.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are here to take care of the country for the long haul.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are but stewards entrusted with the responsibility to take Singapore forward.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The changes that we have made are significant ones.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We made it not because there is an immediate issue that we have to address, but we made it with a view to make sure that issues like these do not come about, especially sensitive issues on race, language and religion.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As the debate in November had highlighted, we will be very happy to be proven wrong, that one of these days we are totally race-blind as we all aspire to be; just like you and for me.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we are all concerned for the future of this country.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What if we are not and what if we are wrong?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Then, it is our responsibility to do what we can to build a mechanism that best allows us to overcome these difficulties should they arise.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If it is for short-term political advantage, let me ask the Members of this House, if we are politicians here calculating our short-term political advantage, would we expend political capital to do this?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: By any measure, any sensible people whom we can talk to, they would know, that such amendments and the moving of this Bill carry with it high political risk, if not political cost.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If this Government led by Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong is for short-term political advantage, would we do it?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Would we expend our political capital to do this?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have no need to do it now because it is not as if we have faced a problem now, but we know the day when we face the problem, we may not have the chance to discuss this calmly as we do now.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I would urge Members of this House not to impute perhaps our own motives on why we are doing this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have gone through this in November and I will repeat this again.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are here to build systems for Singapore for the long haul, not for short-term political advantage, not for the political advantage of any particular parties.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The third set of questions were on the campaign methods for the Presidential Elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government believes, like the taxi driver in Mr Thomas Chua's story, that electing a President is an important matter and that voters should be informed and not cavalier in exercising their vote.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is why we have amended the Act to make sure that prospective candidates have to state that they are aware of the limits set by the Constitution on the role of the President, and they will have no excuse if they decide to mislead the electorate on the proper role of the President.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The voter must vote in an informed fashion.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It would be appropriate here to discuss Mr Ang Wei Neng's question about the statutory declaration that candidates have to make, stating that they understand the role of the Elected President under the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Constitutional Commission cited one observer as saying that it was "misleading and a great disservice to the electorate" when previous candidates promised to pursue particular policies if they were elected into office, despite such areas not being within the constitutional remit of the President's functions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Rahayu alluded to the Commission's recommendations to deal with this and said that she saw merits in the proposals.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The statutory declaration will ensure that the candidate has applied his mind to the Constitutional limits of the Presidency.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It will then be inexcusable if he deliberately chooses to disregard the limits of the Constitution and makes promises or statements exceeding this role.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have put this into the rules, and I take it that anyone who runs for the Presidency should understand the letter of the law and the spirit of the law.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If someone tries to bypass the letter of the law, by violating the spirit of the law, I think I leave it to the good judgement of our electorate.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That means that we have to double our efforts to help all Singaporeans understand the roles prescribed for our Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They are the Singapore Elected Presidency and not the elected presidency of some other countries, with their own unique defined roles.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Singapore Elected Presidency has two main roles.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One, a custodial function for the Reserves and appointments of key appointment holders in the Civil Service.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Two, as a unifying symbol for our nation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These are the two cleared roles for the Elected Presidency of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will also step up educational efforts on the importance of the institution of the Elected President.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As Mr Thomas Chua and Mr Ang Wei Neng had also rightly pointed out, there are fundamental differences between the Presidential Elections and the Parliamentary Elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is also a point made several times in the Constitutional Commission's Report, and attempts to draw parallels between the two can be attributed to persons being ill-informed, or worse, intentionally muddying the waters.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng asked whether we would be increasing the airtime on national TV for candidates, and suggested two televised debates among candidates.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: During Presidential Election 2011, there were two presidential campaign broadcasts for each candidate and one TV roundtable session which involved all four candidates.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The principle that the Government will adhere to is that we will provide candidates with more TV opportunities, which again, I emphasise, will allow for more effective national outreach.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And if I may add, if you just think about it, this actually facilitates and levels the playing field for those without established mechanisms to organise large outreach for themselves.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The details will be made known closer to the elections, and candidates may reach out to voters on a variety of social media platforms, as currently allowed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng asked about whether candidates can continue to meet voters face to face, and if they can organise speeches in places like the indoor stadium.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They can continue to conduct private election meetings at indoor locations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: A meeting is considered private if it is not open to the general public.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: A private meeting will not require a permit under the Public Order Act.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: An example of a private meeting is where it is open to only a limited number of persons who are invited by name to attend the meeting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Candidates can hold such private meetings to engage specific groups of voters.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: No permit from the Police is required for private meetings.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Permits from the Police will be required for meetings that are open to the general public.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These would include election meetings that are organised on or behalf of a candidate and held during the election period, any time on or after Nomination Day but before the eve of Polling Day.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If a candidate intends to have a meeting that is open to the general public at the Indoor Stadium, he will have to obtain a permit from the Police.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng asked for specifics on the interim period between President Tan stepping down at the end of his term and a new President being sworn into office.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: During the interim, the acting President will exercise the powers of the President.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The acting President will have the powers of the President.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Ang suggested that the critics of the Government might have conspiracy theories that the Government will, in this interim period, ask the acting President to exercise his custodial powers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Before I conclude, let me touch on some other points raised by various Members.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Vikram Nair talked about people from mixed parentage.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Yes, indeed, that is point that Mr Thomas Chua has also mentioned.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Should there be such a person, and there would be more, we encourage the Community Committee to adopt an inclusive approach.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, actually, by adopting an inclusive approach, we are allowing more people to be identified with a certain community.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, actually, our approach is quite different from the approach as suggested by some other Members who want to be even more clearly defined as to who forms what community.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If I were to take the House a step back.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: A person identifies himself or herself with that particular community.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And that community accepts that this particular person is from that community.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Once these two conditions are met, the person identifies himself or herself with the community and the community accepts the person as a member of that community, then, we have pretty much met our intent.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the hiatus-triggered mechanism, it will be counted towards that community.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That community would not need to feel shortchanged because someone from that community did not represent them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because in the intervening years, if someone has come forward to be associated with that community, and that community has accepted that person, then that community would have deemed that it has its own representative within the hiatus-triggered mechanism.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are going to adopt an inclusive approach rather than trying to define extra lines, if you like, to do this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On Mr Thomas Chua's point about giving ample notice, and this is the reason why the Government has announced as many of the processes and procedures that we can, as early as possible, for prospective candidates to be familiar with the new processes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The changes that are being made to the Act, such as those pertaining to the Community Committee, are largely consequential to the amendments made to the Constitution that were passed by this House last November.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government is putting in place the final pieces of the changes to the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This set of amendments is the result of the review of the election processes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, we are gathered here to see how best to put in place the nuts and bolts to effect what we have discussed in November.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today is not the occasion for us to reopen the debate.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I thought the Workers' Party's proposal last November was for a Senate, but today, it was on an Appointed President.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is not the occasion for us to do that today.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Based on what we have passed in November, this proposed set of changes is to put in place the nuts and bolts for us to effect the changes that we have agreed to in November.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I spoke at the end of my speech about campaigning methods and the timing of the Presidential Election this year.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These do not require legislative changes, but the Government is of the view that we should announce them as early as possible to give potential candidates ample notice.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This Government has never shied away from acting decisively to strengthen the institutions of the state to ensure a better Singapore for our people.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We proceed to do so because we consider this to be in the best long-term interest of our country, and we will take time to explain the changes to our people.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Throughout the entire process of consultation and changes to the Elected Presidency, the Government has always kept the end goal in mind: ensuring that the Elected President continues to play an important stabiliser role in our system, making sure that our Reserves and our key positions are not compromised, and making sure that the Presidency is not politicised, and making sure that the President continues to be, as it was from its inception in the person of Mr Yusof Ishak, a symbol of our unity for the country.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: With that, Mdm Speaker, I beg to move, and urge all Members to give their support to the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: They just talked about the Minister having to have regard to the general law, to accounting standards but these definitions are not before the House today.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I would like the Minister to comment on whether he agrees with me that, actually, Parliament is not doing what the Constitution (Amendment) Bill has asked us to do with regard to these definitions for private sector candidates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The second clarification concerns the counting of reserved elections.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I think in Parliament in November, the Government has already accused me of the things that Minister Chan Chun Sing has just repeated and I have also answered that in November to say that I am not accusing the Government or the Prime Minister of not telling the truth or that the AGC's advice was not given.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And if the advice from the AGC is such, it would be helpful if the Government could consent to publishing it so that people can understand or try to understand the reasoning.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And the Minister talked about the fact that I am a lawyer and I can understand why clients may want to have confidential communications.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The third point which the Minister made was refuting what I had said was perception of Singaporeans, including myself, that the sudden announcement to count the coming election for President as reserved is in view of what happened at the elections in 2011.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Since the Minister said it is not a short-term purpose, why not?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I do not recall an answer to that.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The last clarification I would like to ask the Minister is in his opening speech earlier, I think he mentioned that both sides of the House agreed in November that there should be a difference between Presidential elections and Parliamentary elections.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I am not sure what he actually meant by that.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: From what I recall, our position has been that the Head of State, we believe, if you want him to be a unifying figure, making him go through elections is inconsistent with that.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I do not think that our Members went on to suggest how the campaign rules of Presidential elections could be refined because we do not believe that the President should go through an election.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What Parliament is doing and asking the Minister to do is to make sure that whatever prevailing accountancy rules that are being practised are adhered to.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That surely is better than what we here, being not in the profession, were to make a set of rules and then have it updated.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think the accountants among us, the people in the financial industry among us, will know that the conventions, rules and practices in the industry evolve.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are setting ourselves, benchmarking ourselves to these high standards that are agreed to by the professional bodies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That, I think, is an even better and stronger set of measures than us setting something in place and having to update it as regularly as what the accounting professions might be capable of.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the second related point, Ms Sylvia Lim asked whether clients can choose to waive the advice and I think I have answered her, which is that, as a lawyer, the Member would know that there will be circumstances where you can choose to release the advice and you can choose not to release the advice and what we have done is no different.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, unless she is going back to challenge and casting doubt on the Prime Minister's integrity, the Prime Minister has stated on record in this House that it has taken advice from the Attorney-General.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We take the Prime Minister for it and it is the Prime Minister's prerogative as to whether he wishes to release the advice as the Member has said.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the third point about the claim that this is a sudden announcement, I would just make two points: one, we have had this debate for a very long time, for more than one year.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We invited the Workers' Party and members of the public to present.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Workers' Party's position was that it would not appear before the Constitutional Commission to present its views, but it will come to this House.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Last year, the Workers' Party came to this House with a proposal for a Senate.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have debated that and we have made our own conclusions and we have moved on from there.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I do not think this is a sudden movement.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second response to the third point that the Member mentioned, Deputy Prime Minister Teo has also shared with this House why we are making the movement now.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the fourth point about the bipartisan support for us to try to depoliticise this, I would just refer Ms Lim to the Hansard, to the speeches made by Mr Leon Perera and I can show them to the Member afterwards which, in so many words, agreed with us that we want a Presidency that is depoliticised.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we should find ways to do so.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And the Government has taken seriously the feedback from this House and the members of the public to see how we can depoliticise the Presidency.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Minister mentioned that there would be regulations drawn up to define how the Community Committee would assess the applicants.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Correct me if I am wrong in this understanding.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But there are two points that I made which the Minister did not address.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: One has to do with the National Service requirement and the second is how community work would be assessed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second question: I would like to press the Minister on this issue of language in the case of a reserved election.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: For example, if a Presidential election has been reserved for the Malay community, would it not be difficult for the Government to agree that Malay, as a language, would be an expectation of any candidate who would stand for that election, up to the level expected of students in schools in the education system?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, on the issue of citizenship, I think I will repeat my point here.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They have the privileges of being a Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They have also the responsibilities of being a Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I think Singaporeans are wise and discerning, so I do not think we need to overly prescribe this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And that has served us well and the same mechanism will continue to work.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the issue of language, I would say that the Community Committee and the respective sub-committees will need to assess the person holistically.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Yes, language will be one of the criteria.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we are also keenly aware that all of us, regardless of our race, language or religion, may practise our religions slightly differently, may live our lifestyles differently.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But the key is this: do the respective Chinese, Malay and Indian sub-committees consider the person belonging to their community, as a package, holistically?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As to how committees work, I would not want to prescribe their roles, and it will  not be my remit to comment on how they should go about doing their function.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The philosophy is that, as a package, do you believe that this person belongs to your community?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I believe that the people in the committees are wise enough to know how to make that judgement call, considering all the factors that the Member has mentioned.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would just like to make a point of clarification to Minister Chan in relation to what he just said.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The speeches I made in November when we had the debate on the Constitution amendment were speeches in support of the Workers' Party's position for an Appointed President, for reverting to an Appointed President and an elected Senate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They were not offering specific suggestions about campaigning procedures for an Elected President.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I was not agreeing with the notion that we should continue to elect the President, and here are my suggestions for the procedures to run that campaign.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I would make the point, since it was brought up by Minster Chan who had made the observation, that the Constitutional Commission agreed with that point as well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Member said that the November speeches were in support of the Appointed President.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I thought the November debate was about the Senate.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How does the Appointed President and Senate proposals work?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, in fact, you are setting that out as a contradiction when there is no contradiction at all.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We argued then for a reversion to an Appointed President and an Elected Senate to handle the custodial role and —

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, can I have it on record that you are now proposing that we have an Appointed President and a Senate?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Not only is it correct, it is what we have argued all along.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, then let me ask this: but you would agree with me that we want a depoliticised President to the extent that our efforts can?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because your line of questioning during November was that we tried our best to have a President that can act as a unifying figure for our country.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Do you share that perspective that we would like a President that can unify us and be depoliticised to the extent possible?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think we do not disagree on the goal of having a unifying President as a symbol for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But what we disagreed about is the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We argued then and we argue again that an election inevitably has a tendency to politicise the office of the President.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: An Appointed President, like what we had in the past, with President Yusof Ishak, like what the Constitutional Commission itself called for, is a better thing for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, the Member wants to appoint a President and a Senate, but as we have gone through in November, that would also have the same risk of politicisation, maybe eight times over.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we are not to go there today but what we can agree I think on both sides of the House is, as the Member has mentioned, to the extent possible, we want a mechanism, an election process that allows us to have a unifying figure and a custodial figure and that is why we have proposed the slight adjustment to the campaigning methods today and I think we can agree on that.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: We do not agree to an election process for the President.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think we can all check the Hansard as to what was said between you and the rest of the debate.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, we are here to put in place the nuts and bolts on how we can get an Elected President, see it working.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I do not have the Hansard with me, but I stood up and I remembered that I agreed with Mr Leon Perera that, indeed, we should look at these things and we would do so when we enact the processes within this Bill and, indeed, that is what we are doing.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I am glad that Mr Perera agreed with me at that point in time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The exact quote was this, "My second question", from Mr Leon Perera, "My second question pertains to a question we have repeated a few times.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What are the strategies that the Government has to mitigate the risk of politicising the unifying office of the President" and it goes on "no doubt the politicisation may not have fully materialised for the past EPs that we have but there is a good reason to believe in future Presidential elections, if let us say, there are 10 candidates and let us say the winner gets 5% of the vote and let us say the campaign ends up becoming bitterly partisan, the office of the President could be politicised." So, it goes on.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And Mr Teo Chee Hean's reply was and I quote, "Turning to the risk of politicisation and a possible tightening of rules for the Presidential Elections, the risk of politicisation is that I have addressed it explicitly just now in my answer but I think what Mr Leon Perera suggests and what the Commission suggests also is to look at the rules and the way that the Presidential Elections are conducted.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think there is merit, and I agree with Mr Leon Perera there." I quote from Mr Teo Chee Hean.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think one of them was touched on in the extract but, inevitably, there will be that risk.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: You can introduce procedural changes to campaign rules and so on and so forth and Minister Chan has shared some of those procedural changes today but it will not eliminate the procedural risk, that is why we argued then and we argue now that an Appointed President, like we had in the past, like President Yusof Ishak, is the best solution for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And when I agreed with Mr Leon Perera, he was listening to me very attentively.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And we all know that Mr Perera, how shall I say, is not shy to stand up to clarify a matter if he has not agreed with it at that point in time.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And at that point in time when I agreed with him that we should make processes to depoliticise the election of the President, he did not respond at that point in time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, I was not arguing that we should go down the path of procedural changes.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Can I read the record for Mr Leon Perera's clarification?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I quote, "My second question pertains to a question we have repeated a few times.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: What are the strategies that the Government has to mitigate the risk of politicising the unifying office of the Presidency?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: No doubt, the politicisation may not have fully materialised for the past EPs that we had.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But there is good reason to believe in future Presidential Elections, if let us say, there are 10 candidates and let us say, the winner gets 5% of the vote, or let us say, the campaign ends up becoming bitterly partisan, the office of the President could be politicised.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I continue, in Mr Leon Perera's words, "I think Ms Rahayu Mahzam came closest to that and to her credit, she talked about tightening up the rules for partisanship during the Presidential Election campaign.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: During the debate, what I did call for was for the Government to explain its strategy for managing the politicisation risk and I felt that whatever had been explained up to that point in time were not sufficient safeguards to manage the politicisation risk.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I alluded to Ms Rahayu Mahzam's comments as being one attempt to explain the strategy, but I pointed to the fact that there had not been a proper strategy explained at that time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think some of the procedural changes that have been suggested today are an attempt to manage that politicisation risk but my statements then cannot be construed to mean that I support an Elected Presidency with procedural changes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What I am saying is that an Elected Presidency inherently has that risk, there is that inevitable tendency.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: There was no comprehensive strategy to manage that, and you can make procedural changes, you can make tweaks here and there but, at the end of the day, an election still runs the risk of becoming politicised even if you make all kinds of procedural changes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: That is why an Appointed Presidency is still a better solution and the Constitutional Commission itself actually pointed that out.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My statements in the November debate did not constitute support of an Elected Presidency with procedural safeguards.

text: But do you wish to record your dissent?
